accepted_examples.german: Ich habe die Informationen direkt von ihm bekommen.
accepted_examples.english: I got the information from him directly.
accepted_examples.note: direkt means directly in the sense of getting information from its source.

accepted_examples.german: Ich kann ein Schiff in der Ferne sehen.
accepted_examples.english: I can see a ship in the distance.
accepted_examples.note: Schiff means a vessel in this sentence.

accepted_examples.german: Der König lud alle auf eine Feier ein.
accepted_examples.english: The king invited everyone to a party.

accepted_examples.german: Hast du danach noch etwas zu tun?
accepted_examples.english: Do you have anything to do after that?
accepted_examples.note: danach refers to what happens after the preceding event or time.

accepted_examples.german: Der Mann hat mir seinen Namen nicht genannt.
accepted_examples.english: That man didn't give me his name.
accepted_examples.note: genannt is the past participle of nennen, used here to say what someone is called or named.

accepted_examples.german: Es brach ein Feuer in der Nähe aus.
accepted_examples.note: Feuer refers to a fire as an event/process.

accepted_examples.german: Tom und Mary erinnern mich an meine Eltern.
accepted_examples.english: Tom and Mary remind me of my parents.
accepted_examples.note: This uses erinnern in the transitive sense to remind someone of a person.

accepted_examples.german: Der See ist an dieser Stelle am tiefsten.
accepted_examples.english: The lake is deepest at this spot.
accepted_examples.note: Stelle means a specific location or spot here.

accepted_examples.german: Viele Kumpel befürchten, dass die Zeche bald geschlossen wird.
accepted_examples.english: Many miners are afraid that the mine will be closed down soon.
accepted_examples.note: Kumpel is used for a miner; this also illustrates its unchanged standard plural.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist wie die Luft, die wir atmen.
accepted_examples.english: It is like the air we breathe.
accepted_examples.note: Luft means ordinary air or atmosphere.

accepted_examples.german: Er scheiterte bei seinem Versuch, den Fluss zu durchschwimmen.
accepted_examples.english: He failed in his attempt to swim across the river.

accepted_examples.german: Ich frage mich, ob ich je heiraten werde.
accepted_examples.english: I wonder if I'll ever get married.
accepted_examples.note: heiraten means to marry or get married.

accepted_examples.german: Du siehst auf diesem Bild echt super aus.
accepted_examples.english: You look great in this picture.

accepted_examples.german: Mein Onkel ruft mich alle drei Tage an.
accepted_examples.english: My uncle calls me every three days.

accepted_examples.german: Es tut mir leid, wir sind total ausverkauft.
accepted_examples.english: I'm sorry, we're completely sold out.
accepted_examples.note: total intensifies the meaning of completely.

accepted_examples.german: Tom hat seinen Hund mit zur Schule gebracht.
accepted_examples.english: Tom brought his dog to school.
accepted_examples.note: gebracht is the Partizip II of bringen and is used with haben.

accepted_examples.german: Es waren nur sechs Leute auf der Party.
accepted_examples.english: There were only six people at the party.

accepted_examples.german: Rom war damals die größte Stadt der Welt.
accepted_examples.english: Rome was the largest city in the world at the time.
accepted_examples.note: damals means at that time in the past.

accepted_examples.german: Ich mache mir genauso viele Sorgen wie du.
accepted_examples.english: I'm just as worried as you are.
accepted_examples.note: genauso viele expresses the same degree or quantity.

held_examples.reason: The German sentence is valid, but the candidate English uses the context-specific, dated word Diet. The replacement uses a clearer translation and the entry meaning is being refined to a formal session.

editorial_examples.english: The committee is meeting on Tuesday.
editorial_examples.note: Duden confirms that tagen is used for holding a session and lists a committee as a typical subject.

entry_updates.note: Duden lists gebracht as the Partizip II of bringen.
This is a verb form, not an adjective; link it to the base lemma bringen.

entry_updates.value: Inflected form: Partizip II of bringen; combines with haben (for example, hat gebracht).
entry_updates.note: Replaces the adjective-only usage note with the checked participle pattern.

entry_updates.value: to hold a formal session; (of a parliament, court, or committee) to meet
entry_updates.note: Duden defines the target sense as holding a meeting or session; a separate impersonal sense means to dawn.

entry_updates.value: Used of a formal body such as a parliament, court, or committee holding a session; tagen also has a separate impersonal sense meaning to dawn.
entry_updates.note: Clarifies the formal-session use shown in the accepted example.

inflected_links.form_note: Partizip II of bringen; combines with haben.

plural_reviews.note: Bälle is the standard plural for a game ball.

plural_reviews.value: No regular plural in the frozen-water sense
plural_reviews.note: Duden marks frozen water as without a plural; servings of ice cream are a separate count expression.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Eis meaning frozen water is normally singular-only. Expressions such as zwei Eis refer to servings of ice cream, not plural ice as frozen water.

plural_reviews.note: Bullen is the plural for a male bovine; it also occurs in several colloquial senses.
Parks is the usual plural, Parke is less common, and Pärke is the usual Swiss variant.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Parks as the usual plural. Parke is less common; Pärke is common in Switzerland.

plural_reviews.note: Taxis is the standard plural; the candidate Taxen is not listed in Duden for this noun.

plural_reviews.value: No regular plural in the usual sea/ocean sense
plural_reviews.note: Duden marks the ordinary sea and sea-state senses as without a plural; Seen belongs to a maritime wave sense or the separate masculine noun for an inland lake.
plural_reviews.usage_note: See meaning the sea or ocean is normally singular-only. Seen usually means inland lakes, or appears in a separate seafaring sense for waves.

plural_reviews.note: The plural is Busse, with double s.
Löcher is the plural for an opening or hole.
Tommys is the plural for the historical term for a British soldier.
Pausen is the standard plural for breaks or pauses.
Hüte is the plural for hats.
Grade is the ordinary plural; Grad remains unchanged in measurement expressions such as 30 Grad.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Grade is used for degrees in general. After a number in temperature or angle measurements, Grad is often unchanged (for example, 30 Grad).

plural_reviews.note: This is a substantivized adjective, so endings vary with case and determiner; the forms are not interchangeable free variants.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Schwarzer is a substantivized adjective. Plural endings depend on grammar: e.g. die Schwarzen with a definite article, but Schwarze without an article. When referring to people, Duden notes the respectful wording Schwarze Menschen.

plural_reviews.note: Mädel and Mädels are standard; Mädeln is a Bavarian and Austrian regional variant.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The common plurals are Mädel and Mädels. Mädeln is regional in Bavaria and Austria.

plural_reviews.note: Themen is the standard plural; Themata is dated/formal and Themas is rarer.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Themen in ordinary German. Themata is dated or formal; Themas is also possible but rarer.

plural_reviews.note: Risiken is standard; Risikos is rare, and Risken is also used in Austria.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Risiken as the normal plural. Risikos is rare; Risken is an Austrian variant.

plural_reviews.note: Knäste is the preferred plural for prison; Duden also records Knaste.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Knäste is the usual plural for a prison. Knaste is an accepted alternative; Knast meaning a prison sentence is singular-only.

plural_reviews.note: Both Fräulein and Fräuleins are listed plurals. The term is dated and should not be used as a form of address unless wanted by the person.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The plural can be Fräulein or Fräuleins. The word is dated; for addressing an adult woman, use Frau unless she prefers Fräulein.

plural_reviews.note: Runden is the standard plural; it also covers rounds of drinks.
Lords refers to people who hold the title; the title itself has no plural.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Lords for people with the title. The title Lord itself is normally singular-only.
